effect_estimate.comment: Purely qualitative comparative process-tracing case study; descriptive contextual numbers (e.g., water bills, watershed spending, farm participation rates, Legionnaires' case counts) are reported in the case narratives, with no statistical effect estimate.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Comparative process tracing of two U.S. municipal water systems under polycentric federalism shows that formal multilevel structure alone does not ensure safe or affordable drinking water; adaptive vs. maladaptive outcomes depend on whether six governance enabling conditions function in practice or are disabled by quiescent rule enforcement, blame avoidance, state receivership, and power/wealth asymmetries. In New York City (1976–present, ~8.4 million residents), active USEPA enforcement of the 1989 Surface Water Treatment Rule via conditional Filtration Avoidance Determinations (1993, 1997, 2007, 2017), upstate lawsuits, gubernatorial mediation, and over $1.5 billion in watershed investments under the 1997 Memorandum of Agreement (130,000 acres of easements; 93% Whole Farm Planning participation across nearly 500 farms by 1998) avoided a $4–6 billion filtration plant while preserving unfiltered water quality and moderate household water bills ($464/year average). In Flint, Michigan (2013–present), state-appointed Emergency Manager rule nullifying local democratic authority, MDEQ regulatory minimalism and misreading of the federal Lead and Copper Rule (blocking corrosion inhibitors), and USEPA Region 5 deference to state primacy (delaying a Safe Drinking Water Act emergency order until January 2016) disabled polycentric checks after the April 2014 switch to the Flint River, producing water 19 times more corrosive than Lake Huron water, fecal coliform boil-water advisories, elevated home water and child blood lead levels, 87 Legionnaires' disease cases in Genesee County over 2 years (vs. 6 and 13 in the prior 2 years), and household water rates nearly double the national average and almost four times Detroit's rates.
